content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of topical ocular prophylaxis for all neonates to prevent gonococcal and chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum. This includes the application of 5% silver nitrate solution, 1% chloramphenicol solution, or 1% chloramphenicol eye ointment. 2. When applying topical treatments to neonates, care must be taken to avoid direct contact with the eye tissue. Additionally, a water-based povidone-iodine solution should be used. 3. The WHO guidelines emphasize that the choice of medication for gonococcal infections may depend on factors such as cost and local resistance patterns to erythromycin, tetracycline, and chloramphenicol. 4. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are a significant global public health issue, causing substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. They directly impact reproductive and child health through complications such as infertility, cancers, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Indirectly, they facilitate the transmission of HIV, further affecting national and individual economies. 5. Globally, over one million curable STIs are acquired daily. In 2016, an estimated 357 million new cases of curable STIs occurred among adults aged 15–49 years, including 131 million cases of chlamydia, 78 million cases of gonorrhea, 6 million cases of syphilis, and 142 million cases of trichomoniasis. 6. Viral STIs, such as herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) and human papillomavirus (HPV), are also highly prevalent. Approximately 417 million people are infected with HSV-2, and 291 million women harbor HPV at any given time. 7. The burden of STIs varies by region and gender, with the highest prevalence in resource-poor countries. If left undiagnosed and untreated, curable STIs can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, fetal loss, and congenital infections. 8. Maternal syphilis infections are estimated to have caused 200,000 stillbirths, neonatal deaths, preterm births, and infected infants in 2016. Curable STIs accounted for the loss of nearly 11 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2013. 9. STIs also have psychological consequences, including stigma, shame, and loss of self-worth. They are associated with relationship disruptions and gender-based violence. 10. Non-ulcerative STIs, such as gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis, increase the risk of HIV transmission by promoting genital shedding of the virus. Effective treatment of STIs is essential to reduce HIV transmission and improve sexual and reproductive health. 11. Updated global treatment guidelines are urgently needed to address the changing patterns of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in STIs, particularly for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Resistance to quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins is increasing, and low-level resistance to nitroimidazoles for Trichomonas vaginalis has been reported. 12. Resistance to azithromycin has been observed in some strains of Treponema pallidum, and treatment failures with tetracyclines and macrolides have been reported for Chlamydia trachomatis. 13. The WHO recommends increasing the dosage of ceftriaxone to 500 mg for the treatment of gonorrhea and continuing to monitor antimicrobial susceptibility. The use of azithromycin in early syphilis should also be reconsidered. 14. The epidemiology of STIs is shifting, with viral pathogens becoming more prevalent than bacterial etiologies for some conditions. Updated information is required to inform locally appropriate prevention and treatment strategies. 15. An increasing proportion of genital ulcers are now caused by viral infections, such as HSV-2, as bacterial infections like chancroid approach elimination in many countries. Treatment guidelines for genital ulcer disease should include HSV-2 management and explore longer treatment durations. 16. Syndromic management of STIs, which involves diagnosing based on consistent symptom groups and easily recognized signs, needs to be updated to reflect the changing situation. Algorithms for vaginal discharge and anorectal infections in key populations, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex workers, are urgently needed. 17. Rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests (POCTs) are transforming STI management. Rapid syphilis tests are widely available, enabling earlier treatment initiation. Efforts are underway to develop POCTs for other STIs to improve syndromic management and identify asymptomatic infections. 18. Updated guidelines should incorporate rapid tests into syndromic management and provide algorithms for testing and screening. These guidelines must address settings with limited access to modern technologies and those where such technologies are available. 19. Countries are strongly encouraged to adopt updated global guidance when establishing standardized national protocols. These protocols should be adapted to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data to ensure effective STI management. 20. Standardized guidelines ensure that all patients receive adequate treatment at every level of healthcare, optimize the training and supervision of healthcare providers, and facilitate the procurement of medicines. 21. The WHO plans a phased approach to updating STI guidelines, addressing a range of infections and issues. Phase 1 will focus on treatment recommendations for specific STIs and urgent issues, while Phase 2 will address STI prevention. These modules will later be consolidated into comprehensive guidelines. 22. Chlamydial infection, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is the most common bacterial STI worldwide, with significant morbidity and economic costs. It is often asymptomatic but can lead to severe complications, particularly in young women, including pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. 23. Rectal and oropharyngeal infections with C. trachomatis are common and often asymptomatic. In pregnancy, chlamydial infection is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. Neonates can acquire the infection during delivery, leading to conjunctivitis and/or nasopharyngeal infection, which may progress to pneumonitis. 24. Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by invasive serovars of C. trachomatis, is a genital ulcer disease that affects lymphoid tissue.
